question: If I get an automatic extension when do I have to file by?
answer:
If you get an automatic extension, you generally have 6 months to file. For a return due April 15, 2026, that means you have until October 15, 2026 [2][4]. The extension gives you more time to file, but not more time to pay. If you don't pay the tax due by the regular due date, you will owe interest [2].

If you're outside the United States and qualify for the automatic 2-month extension, you have until June 15, 2026 (for calendar-year filers) [3]. You can request an additional 4 months, for a total of 6 months, by filing Form 4868 [1]. The deadline in that case is also October 15, 2026 [3].

CORRECT

question: My city added a flat $20 a month trash pickup fee to my property tax bill. Can I deduct it as a real estate tax?
reference: No. A regular charge for a service like trash pickup isn't a real estate tax, even if you pay it to the taxing authority along with your tax bill, so you can't deduct it.
answer:
Generally no. A periodic charge for a residential service, such as a $20 per month trash collection fee charged to each homeowner, is an itemized charge for services and isn't deductible as a real estate tax, even if it's paid to the taxing authority [1][2].

There is an exception. Service charges for things like trash collection are deductible as real estate taxes if all three of these are true [2]:
- The fees are imposed at a like rate against all property in the taxing jurisdiction [2].
- The funds aren't earmarked and are commingled with general revenue funds [2].
- The funds used to maintain or improve services aren't limited to or determined by the amount of the fees collected [2].

Check your real estate tax bill to see whether nondeductible itemized charges are included. If you don't have a copy, ask your taxing authority or mortgage lender for it [2].
judge_reason: CORRECT: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference, that a flat $20 monthly trash fee is generally not deductible as a real estate tax even when paid to the taxing authority. The three-part exception it adds matches IRS guidance and doesn't contradict the reference.

question: I put money into my mortgage escrow account for property taxes. Can I deduct everything that went into escrow?
reference: No. You can only deduct the amount of real estate tax the escrow company actually paid to the taxing authority. If they don't tell you that amount, ask them or the taxing authority.
answer: No. You can deduct only the real estate tax that the third party actually paid to the taxing authority, not the total amount placed in escrow [1][2]. question: If I didn't get a 1099-INT from my bank, do I still have to report the interest I earned?

question: Can I write off money I lost gambling?
reference: Only if you itemize on Schedule A, and only up to the amount of your gambling winnings
answer:
Yes, but only up to the amount of your gambling winnings. You deduct gambling losses on Schedule A (Form 1040), line 16, as an itemized deduction [1]. You can't deduct losses that exceed your winnings [1].

You must report the full amount of your winnings as income, and you can't just subtract your losses and report the difference [1]. You also need to keep an accurate diary or similar record of your winnings and losses [1]. If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040) [4].

question: My husband died in February 2025, a few weeks before he would have turned 65. Can I still get the higher standard deduction for a spouse who is 65 or older?
reference: Only if he was already 65 when he died. The IRS treats someone as turning 65 the day before their 65th birthday, so if he died before that day, he doesn't count as 65 for 2025 and you can't claim the extra amount for him.
answer:
Probably not. If your spouse died in 2025 before reaching age 65, you can't take the higher standard deduction because of your spouse's age [1]. He counts as 65 only if he was 65 or older at the time of death, and a person is considered to reach 65 on the day before their 65th birthday [1][4].

The sources give an example. A spouse born February 14, 1960 who died February 13, 2025 is considered 65. One who died February 12, 2025 is not [1]. Since your husband died weeks before that day, he wouldn't be considered 65 at the end of 2025 [1][4].
